papers.title: f-Divergence Minimization for Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the process of transferring knowledge from a large model to a small one.It has gained increasing attention in the natural language processing community, driven by the demands of compressing evergrowing language models.In this work, we propose an f -DISTILL framework, which formulates sequence-level knowledge distillation as minimizing a generalized f -divergence function.We propose four distilling variants under our framework and show that existing SeqKD and ENGINE approaches are approximations of our f -DISTILL methods.We further derive step-wise decomposition for our f -DISTILL, reducing intractable sequence-level divergence to word-level losses that can be computed in a tractable manner.Experiments across four datasets show that our methods outperform existing KD approaches, and that our symmetric distilling losses can better force the student to learn from the teacher distribution.1

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation
papers.summary: Neural machine translation (NMT) offers a novel alternative formulation of translation that is potentially simpler than statistical approaches.However to reach competitive performance, NMT models need to be exceedingly large.In this paper we consider applying knowledge distillation approaches (Bucila et al., 2006;Hinton et al., 2015) that have proven successful for reducing the size of neural models in other domains to the problem of NMT.We demonstrate that standard knowledge distillation applied to word-level prediction can be effective for NMT, and also introduce two novel sequence-level versions of knowledge distillation that further improve performance, and somewhat surprisingly, seem to eliminate the need for beam search (even when applied on the original teacher model).Our best student model runs 10 times faster than its state-of-the-art teacher with little loss in performance.It is also significantly better than a baseline model trained without knowledge distillation: by 4.2/1.7 BLEU with greedy decoding/beam search.Applying weight pruning on top of knowledge distillation results in a student model that has 13× fewer parameters than the original teacher model, with a decrease of 0.4 BLEU.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Exploring and enhancing the transfer of distribution in knowledge distillation for autoregressive language models
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a technique that compresses large teacher models by training smaller student models to mimic them. The success of KD in auto-regressive language models mainly relies on Reverse KL for mode-seeking and student-generated output (SGO) to combat exposure bias. Our theoretical analyses and experimental validation reveal that while Reverse KL effectively mimics certain features of the teacher distribution, it fails to capture most of its behaviors. Conversely, SGO incurs higher computational costs and presents challenges in optimization, particularly when the student model is significantly smaller than the teacher model. These constraints are primarily due to the immutable distribution of the teacher model, which fails to adjust adaptively to models of varying sizes. We introduce Online Knowledge Distillation (OKD), where the teacher network integrates small online modules to concurrently train with the student model. This strategy abolishes the necessity for on-policy sampling and merely requires minimal updates to the parameters of the teacher's online module during training, thereby allowing dynamic adaptation to the student's distribution to make distillation better. Extensive results across multiple generation datasets show that OKD achieves or exceeds the performance of leading methods in various model architectures and sizes, reducing training time by up to fourfold.

papers.title: Sequence-level Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression of Attention-based Sequence-to-sequence Speech Recognition
papers.summary: We investigate the feasibility of sequence-level knowledge distillation of Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) models for Large Vocabulary Continuous Speech Recognition (LVCSR). We first use a pre-trained larger teacher model to generate multiple hypotheses per utterance with beam search. With the same input, we then train the student model using these hypotheses generated from the teacher as pseudo labels in place of the original ground truth labels. We evaluate our proposed method using Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus. It achieved up to 9.8× parameter reduction with accuracy loss of up to 7.0% word-error rate (WER) increase.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Improving Autoregressive Training with Dynamic Oracles
papers.summary: Many tasks within NLP can be framed as sequential decision problems, ranging from sequence tagging to text generation. However, for many tasks, the standard training methods, including maximum likelihood (teacher forcing) and scheduled sampling, suffer from exposure bias and a mismatch between metrics employed during training and inference. DAgger provides a solution to mitigate these problems, yet it requires a metric-specific dynamic oracle algorithm, which does not exist for many common metrics like span-based F1, ROUGE, and BLEU. In this paper, we develop these novel dynamic oracles and show they maintain DAgger's no-regret guarantee for decomposable metrics like span-based F1. We evaluate the algorithm's performance on named entity recognition (NER), text summarization, and machine translation (MT). While DAgger with dynamic oracle yields less favorable results in our MT experiments, it outperforms the baseline techniques in NER and text summarization.

papers.title: Mask Forcing: Improving Autoregressive Video Diffusion Distillation via Dual-Noise Masking Rollout
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have shown great potential in real-time video generation. Recent methods distill pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into causal AR students through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), but the generated videos often suffer from over-saturation and over-smoothing issues, resulting in limited visual quality and realism. The key contributing factor is the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL objective in DMD, which can cause the student distribution to collapse onto only a few modes of the teacher distribution. To address this, we propose Mask Forcing, a Dual-Noise Masking Rollout strategy that perturbs the AR student self-rollout to mitigate mode collapse induced by reverse-KL mode seeking. The core idea is to inject cleaner signals into noisy rollout inputs via random masks along spatial and temporal axes during the self-rollout process of AR diffusion distillation. Such perturbations encourage the student rollouts to explore more regions of the teacher distribution, allowing DMD to provide learning signals beyond the modes already covered by the student. Moreover, the cleaner tokens act as denoising guidance for other noisier tokens, improving the intermediate rollout predictions and reducing error accumulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method improves multiple AR video diffusion distillation methods with higher visual quality efficiently, without incorporating real video data or additional post-training stages.

papers.title: MiniLLM: On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models
papers.summary: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a promising technique for reducing the high computational demand of large language models (LLMs). However, previous KD methods are primarily applied to white-box classification models or training small models to imitate black-box model APIs like ChatGPT. How to effectively distill the knowledge of white-box LLMs into small models is still under-explored, which becomes more important with the prosperity of open-source LLMs. In this work, we propose a KD approach that distills LLMs into smaller language models. We first replace the forward Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) objective in the standard KD approaches with reverse KLD, which is more suitable for KD on generative language models, to prevent the student model from overestimating the low-probability regions of the teacher distribution. Then, we derive an effective on-policy optimization approach to learn this objective. The student models are named MiniLLM. Extensive experiments in the instruction-following setting show that MiniLLM generates more precise responses with higher overall quality, lower exposure bias, better calibration, and higher long-text generation performance than the baselines. Our method is scalable for different model families with 120M to 13B parameters. Our code, data, and model checkpoints can be found in https://github.com/microsoft/LMOps/tree/main/minillm.

papers.title: Structure-Level Knowledge Distillation For Multilingual Sequence Labeling
papers.summary: Multilingual sequence labeling is a task of predicting label sequences using a single unified model for multiple languages.Compared with relying on multiple monolingual models, using a multilingual model has the benefit of a smaller model size, easier in online serving, and generalizability to low-resource languages.However, current multilingual models still underperform individual monolingual models significantly due to model capacity limitations.In this paper, we propose to reduce the gap between monolingual models and the unified multilingual model by distilling the structural knowledge of several monolingual models (teachers) to the unified multilingual model (student).We propose two novel KD methods based on structure-level information:(1) approximately minimizes the distance between the student's and the teachers' structurelevel probability distributions, (2) aggregates the structure-level knowledge to local distributions and minimizes the distance between two local probability distributions.Our experiments on 4 multilingual tasks with 25 datasets show that our approaches outperform several strong baselines and have stronger zero-shot generalizability than both the baseline model and teacher models.

papers.title: On-Policy Context Distillation for Language Models
papers.summary: Context distillation enables language models to internalize in-context knowledge into their parameters. In our work, we propose On-Policy Context Distillation (OPCD), a framework that bridges on-policy distillation with context distillation by training a student model on its own generated trajectories while minimizing reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence against a context-conditioned teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OPCD on two important applications: experiential knowledge distillation, where models extract and consolidate transferable knowledge from their historical solution traces, and system prompt distillation, where models internalize beneficial behaviors encoded in optimized prompts. Across mathematical reasoning, text-based games, and domain-specific tasks, OPCD consistently outperforms baseline methods, achieving higher task accuracy while better preserving out-of-distribution capabilities. We further show that OPCD enables effective cross-size distillation, where smaller student models can internalize experiential knowledge from larger teachers.

papers.title: Mitigating exposure bias in large language model distillation: an imitation learning approach
papers.summary: Abstract Knowledge distillation is recognized as a valuable model compression strategy that alleviates the computational burden of large language models while preserving performance. This strategy involves training a smaller model utilizing both real data and predictions from a more cumbersome model. Traditional distillation methods, however, are often compromised by exposure bias, which results from reliance on next-step prediction training loss. This bias emerges when models are tested in free-running mode, differing from their training regime and leading to a progressive drift in input distributions between testing and training phases. An analogous issue, known as ‘distributional shift’, has been effectively addressed in imitation learning through various methodologies. Therefore, this paper specifically tailors an imitation learning-based solution to a traditional knowledge distillation framework which inherently considers both real data and the teacher’s predictions as dual sources of expert demonstrations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated over five different test datasets, where it outperforms traditional benchmarks across all evaluation metrics. Specifically, it achieves superior results in perplexity, multi-token generation, and G-Eval score, indicating improvements in both predictive accuracy and alignment with human judgment in text quality. These results underscore the potential of this approach to effectively address exposure bias in large language model distillation.

papers.title: A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models
papers.summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) trains large language models with teacher guidance on student-generated trajectories, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the histories encountered during deployment. As its use expands across language model training, different formulations of supervision and optimization make it difficult to compare methods and understand when they are effective. This survey develops a unified view of OPD through the interplay between student-generated states, teacher information, and policy updates. This framework connects the foundations of distillation with self-distillation, multi-teacher integration, reinforcement learning, and interactive agents. We examine how these settings change the supervision available to the student and relate the resulting design choices to capability transfer, training efficiency, and deployment. Our synthesis centers on the conditions under which guidance remains reliable and learnable as the student evolves, considering both immediate performance and the capacity for subsequent learning. We conclude by discussing open challenges in adapting supervision and allocating computation to support effective learning.

papers.title: Selective Transfer through Sequence Distillation: From Benchmark Knowledge to Backdoor Behaviour
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models, but recent work shows that it can also transfer unintended teacher properties. We study whether different hidden teacher properties survive the same distillation channels. Specifically, we compare two properties: benchmark-associated knowledge and refusal backdoors, and show that distillation treats them very differently. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data successfully pass that knowledge to students through all four distillation channels we test, including when students are trained only on teacher-generated number sequences containing no natural language or domain content whatsoever. Refusal backdoors tell the opposite story: backdoored teachers achieve near-perfect triggered refusal, yet sequence-distilled students inherit essentially none of this behaviour. Logit-based distillation transfers it substantially, reaching up to 85.5\% triggered refusal in students that saw zero backdoor examples. Distillation is therefore selective, and the selection criterion is not what data the student sees, but what structure the teacher's property has. The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.

papers.title: Mutual-learning sequence-level knowledge distillation for automatic speech recognition
Farzi Data: Autoregressive Data Distillation
papers.summary: We study data distillation for auto-regressive machine learning tasks, where the input and output have a strict left-to-right causal structure. More specifically, we propose Farzi, which summarizes an event sequence dataset into a small number of synthetic sequences -- Farzi Data -- which are optimized to maintain (if not improve) model performance compared to training on the full dataset. Under the hood, Farzi conducts memory-efficient data distillation by (i) deriving efficient reverse-mode differentiation of the Adam optimizer by leveraging Hessian-Vector Products; and (ii) factorizing the high-dimensional discrete event-space into a latent-space which provably promotes implicit regularization. Empirically, for sequential recommendation and language modeling tasks, we are able to achieve 98-120% of downstream full-data performance when training state-of-the-art models on Farzi Data of size as little as 0.1% of the original dataset. Notably, being able to train better models with significantly less data sheds light on the design of future large auto-regressive models, and opens up new opportunities to further scale up model and data sizes.

papers.title: Post-Training is About States, Not Tokens: A State Distribution View of SFT, RL, and On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: Large language model post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and distillation are often analyzed through their loss functions: maximum likelihood, policy gradients, forward KL, reverse KL, or related objective-level variants. We study a complementary factor: the state distribution on which supervision is applied. For an autoregressive policy, a state is a prompt plus generated prefix. SFT trains on fixed dataset states, while RL and on-policy distillation (OPD) train on states induced by the current learner. We formalize post-training as state-distribution shaping and run a controlled smallscale study using Qwen3-0.6B-Base on GSM8K, with TruthfulQA and MMLU as retention evaluations. Our results show three phenomena. First, a mild SFT run improves GSM8K with little forgetting, while a stress SFT run causes substantial retention loss. Second, OPD from a degraded SFT teacher surpasses that teacher on GSM8K, TruthfulQA, and MMLU, despite using the teacher as its only supervision source. Third, a lightweight on-policy RL run improves GSM8K while preserving retention. These results support a state-centric view of post-training: the source and locality of training states can be as important as the form of the supervision signal.

papers.title: Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation of Language Models
papers.summary: On-policy distillation is a promising approach for transferring knowledge between language models, where a student learns from dense token-level signals along its own trajectories. This framework typically uses reverse KL divergence, encouraging the student to match the teacher's high-confidence predictions. However, we show that the mode-seeking property of reverse KL reduces generation diversity and yields unstable learning signals when the teacher distribution has high entropy. To address this, we introduce Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation. Our key idea is augmenting the standard reverse KL objective with forward KL when teacher entropy is high, capturing the full range of plausible outputs while retaining precise imitation elsewhere. It balances mode-seeking precision with mode-covering robustness without sacrificing on-policy training efficiency. Experiments show that our method maintains generation diversity (sustained token-level entropy) and improves student-teacher alignment (lower forward KL on high-entropy tokens). Across six math reasoning benchmarks, this yields Pass@8 accuracy gains of +1.37 for Qwen3-0.6B-Base, +2.39 for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, and +5.05 for Qwen3-4B-Base compared to baseline on-policy distillation methods. These results demonstrate that accounting for teacher uncertainty is essential for maintaining diversity and achieving effective knowledge transfer.

papers.title: Investigation of Sequence-level Knowledge Distillation Methods for CTC Acoustic Models
papers.summary: This paper presents knowledge distillation (KD) methods for training connectionist temporal classification (CTC) acoustic models. In a previous study, we proposed a KD method based on the sequence-level cross-entropy, and showed that the conventional KD method based on the frame-level cross-entropy did not work effectively for CTC acoustic models, whereas the proposed method improved the performance of the models. In this paper, we investigate the implementation of sequence-level KD for CTC models and propose a lattice-based sequence-level KD method. Experiments investigating model compression and the training of a noise-robust model using the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) and CHiME4 datasets demonstrate that the sequence-level KD methods improve the performance of CTC acoustic models on both two tasks, and show that the lattice-based method can compute the sequence-level KD more efficiently than the N-best-based method proposed in our previous work.

review.overview:
The papers split along one axis: which state (prefix) distribution supervision is applied on. Off-policy KD trains on fixed prefixes: ground truth for word-level KD, or teacher-generated sequences for SeqKD [arXiv:1606.07947] and its speech variants [arXiv:1811.04531][doi:10.1109/icassp.2019.8682671][doi:10.1016/j.neucom.2020.11.025]. On-policy KD trains on prefixes sampled from the student, with teacher feedback; it began as imitation-learning/DAgger-style distillation [arXiv:2009.07253][doi:10.1007/s00521-025-11162-0][arXiv:2406.09393] and was popularized for LLMs [arXiv:2306.13649][arXiv:2306.08543]. A second, often confounded axis is the divergence used: forward KL, reverse KL, JSD or TVD [arXiv:2307.15190][arXiv:2603.07079][arXiv:2409.12512]. Recent work tries to separate the two axes explicitly [arXiv:2605.22731v1] and survey it [arXiv:2604.00626].

Three points matter for the reader's setting: a small multimodal transduction task (L6-A8) scored by val_invalid_rate. First, almost all evidence comes from NLP/LLM benchmarks scored by ROUGE, BLEU or accuracy, not by structural validity of outputs. Second, the claimed on-policy advantage (exposure-bias correction) depends on student capacity, teacher–student gap and teacher entropy. These conditions are rarely varied systematically, and [arXiv:2409.12512] reports that on-policy training gets harder when the student is much smaller. Third, the reverse-KL mode-seeking that on-policy methods typically pair with is itself contested [arXiv:2603.07079][arXiv:2609.09123]. A 'validity' metric may reward mode-seeking (fewer malformed outputs) even where coverage suffers. That makes the reader's metric a useful, under-studied lens.

themes.name: Off-policy sequence-level distillation (teacher-generated or fixed data)
themes.summary: The student is trained on teacher beam outputs or ground-truth prefixes with word- or sequence-level losses. SeqKD showed that training on teacher modes simplifies the target distribution and works well for NMT and ASR. It is cheap because teacher outputs can be precomputed. Its weakness is that the student never sees its own errors at training time.

themes.name: Imitation-learning view: exposure bias and DAgger-style distillation
themes.summary: Distillation is framed as imitation learning, with the teacher acting as an oracle queried on student-visited states. Mixing student rollouts with teacher labels reduces distribution drift in free-running decoding. Dynamic oracles extend DAgger to sequence metrics.

themes.name: On-policy distillation for LLMs (GKD, MiniLLM and successors)
themes.summary: The student samples its own outputs and receives token-level teacher feedback, usually under reverse KL or generalized JSD. GKD interpolates between fixed and student-generated data through a mixing fraction, which is directly a knob for on- vs off-policy. MiniLLM uses policy-gradient optimization of reverse KL. Later work extends the idea to context distillation.

themes.name: Divergence choice and its interaction with sampling
themes.summary: Forward KL (mode-covering) and reverse KL (mode-seeking), along with f-divergence generalizations, yield different students. Several papers argue that reverse KL fails to capture most teacher behavior or collapses diversity when teacher entropy is high. They propose hybrids such as entropy-gated FKL+RKL or noise-perturbed rollouts.

themes.name: Disentangling state distribution from objective
themes.summary: These works argue that the key variable is the distribution of prefixes on which supervision is applied, not the loss. They run controlled small-scale comparisons of SFT, RL and on-policy distillation.

themes.name: What transfers through distillation channels
themes.summary: These works study which teacher properties (knowledge, backdoors) survive different distillation channels, and how synthetic data can stand in for real data in autoregressive training. They are relevant to whether off-policy teacher data carries the target property at all.

paper_notes.contribution: Introduces word-level and sequence-level KD (training on teacher beam outputs) for NMT. Shows that SeqKD lets a small student match much of the teacher and can even remove the need for beam search. This is the canonical off-policy baseline.
paper_notes.limitation: The student is trained only on teacher prefixes, so exposure bias is untreated. It offers no analysis of when training on the teacher's mode helps or hurts, beyond NMT/BLEU.

paper_notes.contribution: GKD trains on a mixture of fixed and student-generated sequences with flexible divergences (FKL, RKL, generalized JSD). It shows on-policy data generally helps on summarization, translation and arithmetic reasoning. Its student-data fraction is the most direct experimental knob for on- vs off-policy.
paper_notes.limitation: Optimal divergence and mixing ratio are task-dependent and chosen empirically. There is no predictive account of when on-policy wins, and experiments use T5-scale NLP tasks with quality metrics rather than validity/structural-error metrics.

paper_notes.contribution: MiniLLM argues for reverse KL for generative LLM distillation and optimizes it with policy gradient on student samples, including variance-reduction tricks. It reports better calibration and fewer degenerate long generations.
paper_notes.limitation: The gains mix two factors, RKL and on-policy sampling, which are not cleanly ablated. Policy-gradient training adds variance and cost, and the evaluation focuses on instruction following.

paper_notes.contribution: Casts autoregressive KD as imitation learning with the teacher as oracle on student-visited states. It outperforms SeqKD on translation and summarization.
paper_notes.limitation: It predates LLM-scale on-policy work, and the comparison covers a limited range of student/teacher size gaps. It is not analyzed under divergence choice.

paper_notes.contribution: The f-DISTILL framework unifies SeqKD and ENGINE as approximations of f-divergence minimization. It derives step-wise decompositions and compares KL, RKL, JS and TVD variants.
paper_notes.limitation: It focuses on the objective rather than the sampling distribution. Whether a given divergence's benefit persists under on- vs off-policy sampling is not systematically crossed.

paper_notes.contribution: Argues that RKL mimics only some teacher features. It finds that student-generated outputs are costly and hard to optimize when the student is much smaller than the teacher, and proposes remedies.
paper_notes.limitation: The evidence is LLM-specific. The capacity-gap threshold at which on-policy stops helping is not quantified as a curve.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows that RKL-based on-policy distillation reduces diversity and gives unstable signals when teacher entropy is high. Adds forward KL selectively on high-entropy tokens.
paper_notes.limitation: The entropy gate is heuristic. Results concern LM tasks where diversity matters, and the effect on validity-type metrics is unexplored.

paper_notes.contribution: Controlled study (Qwen3-0.6B, GSM8K) that formalizes post-training as state-distribution shaping. It separates the effect of which prefixes are supervised from the loss used.
paper_notes.limitation: Single small model and a single task. Whether its conclusions hold for non-language transduction or for different teacher-student gaps is untested.

paper_notes.contribution: Survey that unifies on-policy distillation methods around student states, teacher information and policy updates. Useful for situating method variants.
paper_notes.limitation: A survey adds no new controlled evidence, and its comparisons inherit the heterogeneity of the underlying papers.

paper_notes.contribution: Extends on-policy RKL distillation to context distillation, where the teacher is the same model conditioned on extra context.
paper_notes.limitation: Different setting: the teacher and student share capacity, so lessons about capacity gaps do not transfer.

paper_notes.contribution: Imitation-learning approach to mitigating exposure bias in LLM distillation.
paper_notes.limitation: Abstract-level evidence only. Its relation to GKD/MiniLLM and the controls used are unclear.

paper_notes.contribution: Builds dynamic oracles for DAgger on metrics such as span F1, ROUGE and BLEU, preserving no-regret guarantees for decomposable metrics.
paper_notes.limitation: Not distillation per se: the oracle is metric-derived rather than a teacher model. Guarantees are limited to decomposable metrics.

paper_notes.contribution: Applies SeqKD with multiple beam hypotheses to attention-based ASR, achieving 9.8x compression.
paper_notes.limitation: Off-policy only, with a WER cost of up to 7%. There is no comparison with student-sampled training.

paper_notes.contribution: Lattice-based sequence-level KD for CTC acoustic models. Shows that frame-level KD fails for CTC while sequence-level KD works.
paper_notes.limitation: Specific to CTC (non-autoregressive alignment), so it is only indirectly informative for autoregressive on-policy questions.

paper_notes.contribution: Identifies RKL mode-seeking as the cause of over-saturation in autoregressive video diffusion distillation. Perturbs student self-rollouts with dual-noise masking.
paper_notes.limitation: Diffusion/video domain. Its rollout perturbation idea has not been tested for discrete token transduction.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows that different teacher properties transfer very differently through the same distillation channels, with benchmark knowledge surviving even via number sequences.
paper_notes.limitation: About what transfers, not about on- vs off-policy efficiency. The channels are not mapped onto student-sampled training.

gaps.gap: No study maps when on-policy beats off-policy as a function of student capacity relative to the teacher. A grid over student size × student-data fraction (GKD λ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1}) on a fixed transduction task, measuring val_invalid_rate, would directly answer the reader's question.
gaps.why_open: GKD tunes the mixing ratio per task, and [arXiv:2409.12512] reports that on-policy degrades with large capacity gaps. Neither produces a crossover curve.

gaps.gap: The sampling distribution (on vs off) and the divergence (FKL vs RKL vs JSD) are confounded in most comparisons. A full 2×3 factorial at matched compute would show whether 'on-policy helps' is actually 'RKL helps' or vice versa.
gaps.why_open: MiniLLM changes both at once. f-DISTILL varies only the divergence, and the state-distribution study varies only states on a single LM task.

gaps.gap: Effect on structural validity/invalid-output rate rather than quality scores. Mode-seeking objectives and on-policy correction of self-generated errors both plausibly reduce invalid outputs. However, no paper uses invalid rate as the primary metric or checks whether it tracks BLEU/accuracy.
gaps.why_open: The evaluated metrics are BLEU, ROUGE, WER and GSM8K accuracy. The diversity-collapse critiques imply validity and coverage may trade off, but this is unmeasured.

gaps.gap: Teacher entropy as a predictor of which regime wins. Measuring per-example teacher entropy on the multimodal task, and checking whether off-policy SeqKD (teacher mode) or on-policy FKL/RKL gives a lower invalid rate per entropy bucket, would give a 'when' rule.
gaps.why_open: Entropy-aware OPD gates the loss by entropy but does not compare against off-policy distillation per entropy bucket. SeqKD's simplification argument is likewise untested by entropy.

gaps.gap: Compute-matched comparison: on-policy requires student sampling plus teacher scoring at every step, while SeqKD precomputes the teacher outputs once. No paper reports invalid rate vs total FLOPs or wall-clock for both.
gaps.why_open: Papers report final-quality numbers at different budgets. [arXiv:2409.12512] notes the cost of student-generated outputs but gives no Pareto curve.

gaps.gap: Schedules from off- to on-policy: whether warm-starting with SeqKD and then switching to on-policy beats either pure regime, and when to switch. Instance-ordering curricula exist, but not data-source curricula.
gaps.why_open: DAgger-style mixing and GKD's fixed λ are static or follow a simple anneal. The curriculum work orders instances, not the policy that generates them.

gaps.gap: Rollout perturbation for discrete on-policy distillation. Mask Forcing's noisy self-rollouts reduce mode collapse in video, but noise or masking on student token prefixes is untested for text or multimodal transduction.
gaps.why_open: The method is demonstrated only for diffusion video, and the discrete analogue (e.g., random token corruption of student prefixes) has not been compared with clean on-policy training.

gaps.gap: Whether on-policy advantages appear for non-language or multimodal transduction at small scale. Speech work stayed off-policy, and on-policy work is almost all text LLMs.
gaps.why_open: The ASR/CTC KD papers never tried student-sampled training. The only controlled state-distribution study is GSM8K text.

trends: The field shifted from off-policy SeqKD (2016–2020, NMT/ASR) to on-policy distillation as the default for LLMs (2023 onward), reframed through imitation learning and exposure bias.
Reverse KL became the default objective paired with on-policy sampling, and recent work questions its mode-seeking side effects, moving toward hybrid FKL/RKL or entropy-adaptive objectives.
There is growing effort to disentangle the state distribution from the loss, with controlled small-scale studies and unifying surveys replacing method-versus-method leaderboard comparisons.
The on-policy idea is spreading to new settings (context distillation, agents, autoregressive video diffusion), while evidence in non-text discrete transduction remains thin.
Cost and capacity-gap limits of on-policy distillation are increasingly acknowledged but not yet quantified as decision rules.

ideas.title: Invalid-rate-triggered off-to-on switch, with yoked-step and corrupted-prefix controls
ideas.description: Train the student off-policy at first (on_policy_frac=0, teacher or ground-truth prefixes). Then raise on_policy_frac to a target value (0.5 or 1.0) once the student's running free-run invalid rate, measured on a small held-out training probe batch every 100 steps, drops below a threshold tau. Two controls test why the trigger works. The first is a yoked fixed-step control: for each seed, a separate run switches at the exact step where the adaptive run fired. If the yoked run matches the adaptive run, the trigger's only value is locating a good step offline. If the adaptive run is better, the online response to the student's own state matters. The second is a discriminating negative control aimed at the exposure-bias explanation. After the same trigger, the run replaces student rollouts with ground-truth prefixes that are randomly token-corrupted, at a rate matched to the student's current per-token error rate. If this matches true on-policy, the late-phase gain comes from generic prefix noise (a robustness effect) rather than from teacher correction of the student's own errors.
ideas.gap: Gap 6 (schedules from off- to on-policy and when to switch), with secondary relevance to gap 3 (invalid rate as the primary metric).

hypothesis.claim: A switch triggered by the student's own invalid rate achieves lower val_invalid_rate than pure off-policy, pure on-policy, and fixed-step switches. The benefit requires student-generated prefixes: corrupted-ground-truth prefixes at matched error rate should not reproduce it.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Adaptive switch (best tau) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1.0 point below the better pure regime, averaged over 5 seeds, and below the 8.8 baseline. The yoked fixed-step run is within noise of or worse than adaptive. The corrupted-prefix control recovers less than half of the adaptive gain over pure off-policy.

ideas.experiment_plan: Use default d_model=32, n_layers=2, steps=3000, lr=0.003, temperature=1.0, and 5 seeds per arm on multimodal-transduction-L6-A8. Arms: (A) on_policy_frac=0 throughout. (B) on_policy_frac=1.0 throughout. (C) GKD-style static on_policy_frac=0.5. (D) fixed-step switches at 750, 1500 and 2250. (E) adaptive trigger with tau in {40%, 25%, 15%} on a 256-example probe batch, switching to frac in {0.5, 1.0}; set a 1500-step cap and force the switch if the trigger has not fired. (F) yoked fixed-step switch at E's firing step, with a different seed. (G) the same trigger as E, but post-switch prefixes are ground truth with random token substitution at a rate matched to the student's measured per-token error. The loss stays the default divergence across all arms, so the sampling distribution is the only factor varied. Implement this as a schedule edit plus a data-source edit for G. Report the final val_invalid_rate, the invalid-rate trajectory and the trigger step. Count total forward passes so compute can be compared across arms.
ideas.novelty_rationale: In the reviewed works, mixing between fixed and student data is static (GKD λ) or follows a simple anneal (DAgger-style). Curriculum work orders instances rather than the data-generating policy. None of these papers conditions the switch on the student's own validity, separates trigger responsiveness from step location with a yoked control, or tests corrupted prefixes against student prefixes at matched error rate. Mask Forcing perturbs rollouts in video only. This is based on the reviewed set, not an exhaustive search.

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Mask Forcing: Improving Autoregressive Video Diffusion Distillation via Dual-Noise Masking Rollout
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have shown great potential in real-time video generation. Recent methods distill pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into causal AR students through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), but the generated videos often suffer from over-saturation and over-smoothing issues, resulting in limited visual quality and realism. The key contributing factor is the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL objective in DMD, which can cause the student distribution to collapse onto only a few modes of the teacher distribution. To address this, we propose Mask Forcing, a Dual-Noise Masking Rollout strategy that perturbs the AR student self-rollout to mitigate mode collapse induced by reverse-KL mode seeking. The core idea is to inject cleaner signals into noisy rollout inputs via random masks along spatial and temporal axes during the self-rollout process of AR diffusion distillation. Such perturbations encourage the student rollouts to explore more regions of the teacher distribution, allowing DMD to provide learning signals beyond the modes already covered by the student. Moreover, the cleaner tokens act as denoising guidance for other noisier tokens, improving the intermediate rollout predictions and reducing error accumulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method improves multiple AR video diffusion distillation methods with higher visual quality efficiently, without incorporating real video data or additional post-training stages.

papers.title: Mitigating exposure bias in large language model distillation: an imitation learning approach
papers.summary: Abstract Knowledge distillation is recognized as a valuable model compression strategy that alleviates the computational burden of large language models while preserving performance. This strategy involves training a smaller model utilizing both real data and predictions from a more cumbersome model. Traditional distillation methods, however, are often compromised by exposure bias, which results from reliance on next-step prediction training loss. This bias emerges when models are tested in free-running mode, differing from their training regime and leading to a progressive drift in input distributions between testing and training phases. An analogous issue, known as ‘distributional shift’, has been effectively addressed in imitation learning through various methodologies. Therefore, this paper specifically tailors an imitation learning-based solution to a traditional knowledge distillation framework which inherently considers both real data and the teacher’s predictions as dual sources of expert demonstrations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated over five different test datasets, where it outperforms traditional benchmarks across all evaluation metrics. Specifically, it achieves superior results in perplexity, multi-token generation, and G-Eval score, indicating improvements in both predictive accuracy and alignment with human judgment in text quality. These results underscore the potential of this approach to effectively address exposure bias in large language model distillation.

papers.title: DASH-OPD: Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: While on-policy distillation (OPD) reduces exposure bias by training student language models on their own rollouts, early student errors in long-horizon agentic scenarios can lead to contexts unfamiliar to the teacher. To improve trajectory quality, recent work on agentic OPD introduces teacher intervention into training rollouts by switching the executor between the student and the teacher. However, existing methods determine how much teacher intervention is needed---but not when. To address this limitation, we propose DASH-OPD (Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for OPD), the first agentic OPD method to perform adaptive, bidirectional executor switching. At each turn, DASH-OPD measures teacher--student discrepancy using a mean log-likelihood ratio over action tokens. High student-to-teacher ratios on student turns serve as drift signals, while low teacher-to-student ratios on teacher turns serve as recovery signals. These signals are accumulated over multiple turns to form drift and recovery evidence, respectively. DASH-OPD switches executors when either type of evidence exceeds its corresponding switching threshold, introducing hysteresis that prevents rapid switching triggered by transient discrepancy fluctuations. Across three benchmarks and two student model scales, DASH-OPD outperforms five baselines in all 14 task-performance comparisons, while requiring the fewest interaction turns in nine of ten efficiency comparisons. Code, trained models, and training logs are available at https://github.com/Lucian1115/DASH-OPD

papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.

ideas.title: Invalid-rate-triggered switch from off-policy to on-policy distillation versus fixed-step switches
ideas.description: Turn GKD's static student-data fraction into a feedback-controlled schedule. Training starts fully off-policy (on_policy_frac=0, word-level KD on fixed or teacher prefixes). Every 50 steps the script measures the invalid rate of a small batch of student rollouts generated at the training temperature. When that rollout invalid rate stays below a threshold tau for two consecutive checks, on_policy_frac ramps over 200 steps to a target lambda_on. The mechanism comes from DAgger's mixing coefficient beta in imitation-learning KD, which decides when the learner's own states are good enough to supervise. Here beta is driven by a measured competence signal rather than decayed by step count. The comparison set has three groups: (a) pure off-policy, (b) pure on-policy at several fractions, and (c) fixed-step switches at 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000 steps. This tests whether the switch time matters, and whether tying it to the student's own invalid rate beats a well-chosen fixed step.

hypothesis.claim: On-policy supervision helps only once student rollouts are near-valid. Earlier, garbage prefixes waste teacher signal, as the capacity-gap difficulty reported in arXiv:2409.12512 suggests. A switch triggered by rollout invalid rate should therefore beat both pure regimes and match or beat the best fixed-step switch without per-task tuning.

papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. ideas.title: Invalid-rate-triggered switch from SeqKD to on-policy distillation versus fixed-step switches
ideas.description: Training starts fully off-policy (on_policy_frac=0, teacher-generated or ground-truth prefixes). A running estimate of the student's batch invalid rate on its own greedy rollouts is tracked every 50 steps. When it falls below a threshold tau, on_policy_frac is ramped to a target value lambda_on over a short window. This adaptive trigger is compared against a grid of fixed-step switches and against both pure regimes. The proposed mechanism is that early on-policy rollouts are mostly malformed, so teacher feedback on them is spent on states the converged student never visits; that gradient is off-target and noisy. Once rollouts are near-valid, the states the student visits overlap with its eventual test-time states, and only then does exposure-bias correction pay off. If this is right, the best switch point should line up with a student invalid-rate level, not with a step count.
ideas.gap: Gap 6 (off-to-on data-source schedules and when to switch), and as a side effect gap 3 (invalid rate as the primary metric).

hypothesis.claim: A schedule that switches from off- to on-policy when the student's own rollout invalid rate drops below a threshold gives lower val_invalid_rate than pure off-policy, pure on-policy, and the best fixed-step switch. The optimal fixed switch step should move with student capacity in a way that the invalid-rate trigger tracks automatically.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Adaptive trigger (tau around 30%) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1.0 point below the best of {pure off, pure on, best fixed switch}, averaged over 5 seeds, and beats the 8.8 baseline. Across d_model in {16,32,64}, the best fixed switch step varies by more than 2x, while the best tau varies by at most one grid level.

ideas.experiment_plan: Edit the schedule so that on_policy_frac(t) is a function of the monitored invalid rate. Every 50 steps, greedy-decode 64 training inputs with the student and score them with the task validity checker. Arms, with 5 seeds each, steps=3000, and lr/temperature at defaults unless stated: (a) on_policy_frac=0; (b) on_policy_frac=1 from step 0; (c) constant on_policy_frac=0.5; (d) fixed switch at steps {300,750,1500,2250}, ramping 0 to 1 over 100 steps; (e) adaptive trigger with tau in {60,30,15}% and the same ramp; (f) a matched control that replays the switch step each seed of arm (e) actually used, but as a fixed step. Arm (f) separates the benefit of the trigger's timing from its per-seed adaptivity. Repeat (a), (b), (d-best) and (e-best) at d_model {16,64} to test whether the optimum moves with capacity. Use the same loss in every arm (token-level FKL on teacher logits at temperature 1) so the divergence is held fixed. Report val_invalid_rate, the switch step, and wall-clock.
ideas.novelty_rationale: GKD uses a fixed lambda, and the DAgger-style KD in [arXiv:2009.07253] uses a fixed or annealed mixing. Neither conditions the data source on the student's measured rollout quality, nor reports how the switch point depends on capacity. Absence in this review does not prove it is untried elsewhere; the novelty queries below target that.

novelty_review.summary:
From the abstracts alone, no retrieved paper gates the off-to-on-policy data-source fraction on the student's measured rollout invalid rate, or tests whether the switch point tracks capacity. This is only a provisional difference, not verified novelty.

The closest overlap is DTDD. It shares the core mechanistic premise: on-policy supervision is unreliable when the student strays far from the teacher. It also uses an adaptive, student-state-based trigger. However, DTDD triggers teacher takeover inside rollouts based on divergence, rather than scheduling the data-source mix on validity.

Other overlaps are partial:
- GKD and the imitation-learning KD papers share the exposure-bias rationale for on-policy data.
- CPD and POCL share progressive teacher-to-student scheduling, but schedule on difficulty or fixed intervals.
- OKD supports the capacity-dependence assumption.

The abstracts do not reveal whether GKD's lambda or DAgger-style mixing is fixed, annealed or adaptive. The novelty rationale's claims about them need full-text checking.

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Calibrated Progressive Distillation: Co-Designing Curriculum and Target Mixing for Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a key technique for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet it faces challenges stemming from the teacher-student capacity gap.While existing KD methods address these challenges either by mixing teacher and student distributions in the distillation target or by using curriculum learning to sequence training from easy to hard examples, they typically design these two strategies independently, missing the opportunity for synergistic co-design.To bridge this gap, we propose Calibrated Progressive Distillation (CPD), a white-box KD framework that co-designs curriculum scheduling and target mixing through a unified difficulty-aware principle.CPD uses a difficulty profile to select epoch-specific subsets that ensure a uniform increase in average difficulty, adapting to the dataset's intrinsic hardness structure.Simultaneously, the mixing coefficient in the distillation target and the distillation temperature are synchronized with this progression, gradually shifting supervision from teacher-dominated to student-informed signals as training advances.Theoretically, CPD ensures bounded gradients and induces an implicit attention shift from easy to hard samples.Empirically, CPD consistently outperforms advanced KD methods across diverse tasks, while reducing training runtime by over 10%.Our work demonstrates that aligning data scheduling with distillation signal design is crucial for effective and efficient LLM distillation.

papers.title: SLaM: Student-Label Mixing for Distillation with Unlabeled Examples
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation with unlabeled examples is a powerful training paradigm for generating compact and lightweight student models in applications where the amount of labeled data is limited but one has access to a large pool of unlabeled data. In this setting, a large teacher model generates ``soft'' pseudo-labels for the unlabeled dataset which are then used for training the student model. Despite its success in a wide variety of applications, a shortcoming of this approach is that the teacher's pseudo-labels are often noisy, leading to impaired student performance. In this paper, we present a principled method for knowledge distillation with unlabeled examples that we call Student-Label Mixing (SLaM) and we show that it consistently improves over prior approaches by evaluating it on several standard benchmarks. Finally, we show that SLaM comes with theoretical guarantees; along the way we give an algorithm improving the best-known sample complexity for learning halfspaces with margin under random classification noise, and provide the first convergence analysis for so-called ``forward loss-adjustment" methods.

papers.title: Being Strong Progressively! Enhancing Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models through a Curriculum Learning Framework
papers.summary: Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses large language models (LLMs) by transferring the teacher model's capabilities to a smaller student model, reducing inference cost and memory usage while maintaining performance. However, existing KD methods for LLMs often fail to prevent significant shifts in the student model's distribution during training, leading to issues such as catastrophic forgetting, mode collapse, and training-inference mismatch. To address these challenges, we propose a novel, plug-in curriculum learning framework inspired by the strength training principle of "progressive overload" (POCL), which can be seamlessly integrated into existing white-box KD approaches with minimal computational overhead. The framework comprises two core components: (1) a difficulty measurer that ranks and partitions training samples from easy to hard, and (2) a training scheduler that incrementally introduces these subsets into the distillation process at fixed intervals while applying loss functions with progressively rising temperatures. By starting with the easiest samples and progressively increasing the difficulty, the approach enhances both the stability and efficiency of learning. Extensive experiments in instruction-following settings demonstrate that POCL consistently improves the performance of distilled student models across various white-box KD methods and model families. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of sorted training samples in KD for LLMs. More generally, our work demonstrates how to structure training data within the KD process to enhance the stability and performance of distilled LLMs.

ideas.title: Valid-prefix-truncated mixed rollouts: a token-level self-pacing off-to-on curriculum
ideas.description: This replaces the global switch with a per-example curriculum. Each rollout is sampled from the student, but only up to its first position where the prefix becomes invalid; the checker is applied incrementally. From that position the teacher continues the sequence, and the student is trained with teacher-logit FKL on the whole spliced sequence. Early in training most of each sequence is teacher-generated, which is effectively off-policy. As the student improves, the student-generated fraction grows automatically, so the data source shifts from off- to on-policy at the granularity of each example. The mechanism under test is that garbage tails of student rollouts, not student prefixes in general, are what make early on-policy training harmful. A random-truncation control at matched student-prefix length distinguishes 'validity-aware truncation' from 'shorter student prefixes'.
ideas.gap: Gap 6 (data-source curriculum, here per-token), and it also probes gap 7 (prefix perturbation or correction in discrete on-policy distillation).

hypothesis.claim: Truncating student rollouts at the first invalid prefix and splicing in teacher continuations lowers val_invalid_rate below both pure regimes and below a global invalid-rate-triggered switch. The benefit comes specifically from removing post-error states, not from shortening the student prefix.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Validity-truncated splicing beats pure off-policy by at least 1.5 points and pure on-policy by a wider margin. The random-truncation arm with matched student-prefix length recovers less than half of that gain. The student-prefix fraction rises monotonically during training without being scheduled.

ideas.experiment_plan: Edit the augmentation/loss so that each training batch is built from student samples (temperature knob in {0.7,1.0}). Run the validity checker on prefixes and truncate at the first violation; if the task checker only scores full sequences, use the earliest position at which no valid completion exists under the task grammar. Then append a teacher greedy continuation and apply token-level FKL to teacher logits over all positions. Arms, 5 seeds each, d_model=32, steps=3000: (a) pure off (on_policy_frac=0); (b) pure on (on_policy_frac=1); (c) the best global switch from idea 1, or a fixed switch at 1500 if idea 1 is not yet run; (d) valid-prefix splicing; (e) random-truncation splicing, cutting each rollout at a position drawn from the per-step empirical distribution of arm (d)'s cut points; (f) splicing but with the loss masked to the student-prefix positions only, to test whether the teacher tail itself contributes. Log the student-prefix fraction over time and val_invalid_rate. Optionally repeat (a), (b), (d) and (e) at d_model=16, where the capacity gap is larger.
ideas.novelty_rationale: DAgger-style KD and GKD use whole student rollouts or whole fixed sequences. Mask Forcing perturbs rollouts with noise in continuous video. None of the reviewed papers truncates discrete rollouts at a structural-validity boundary and hands control to the teacher, or controls with random truncation at matched length. Novelty is unverified beyond this review.

novelty_review.summary: The core components (on-policy rollouts with teacher feedback, imitation-learning-style mixing of student and teacher control, and truncating student rollouts during early training) are each present in the retrieved abstracts. Truncated/Progressive OPD (arXiv:2605.31490) is the closest match: it truncates student rollouts and expands the horizon over training, motivated by unreliable late-position feedback early in training. Its stated cut criterion is horizon control, not a structural-validity boundary, and its abstract does not mention a teacher continuation splice. SPTA (arXiv:2611.03133) shares the premise that erroneous student prefixes degrade teacher supervision, but it adapts the teacher instead of truncating. The DAgger-style KD abstracts (2009.07253, doi:10.1007/s00521-025-11162-0) likely involve mixed student/teacher roll-in, but their abstracts give no details. What these abstracts do not show is the specific combination: a validity-triggered cut, a teacher-generated tail, and a random-truncation control matched on cut length. That is only a provisional distinction. Overall the overlap is substantial at the mechanism level (rollout truncation as an off-to-on curriculum), so the status is overlap.
