papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Mask Forcing: Improving Autoregressive Video Diffusion Distillation via Dual-Noise Masking Rollout
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have shown great potential in real-time video generation. Recent methods distill pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into causal AR students through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), but the generated videos often suffer from over-saturation and over-smoothing issues, resulting in limited visual quality and realism. The key contributing factor is the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL objective in DMD, which can cause the student distribution to collapse onto only a few modes of the teacher distribution. To address this, we propose Mask Forcing, a Dual-Noise Masking Rollout strategy that perturbs the AR student self-rollout to mitigate mode collapse induced by reverse-KL mode seeking. The core idea is to inject cleaner signals into noisy rollout inputs via random masks along spatial and temporal axes during the self-rollout process of AR diffusion distillation. Such perturbations encourage the student rollouts to explore more regions of the teacher distribution, allowing DMD to provide learning signals beyond the modes already covered by the student. Moreover, the cleaner tokens act as denoising guidance for other noisier tokens, improving the intermediate rollout predictions and reducing error accumulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method improves multiple AR video diffusion distillation methods with higher visual quality efficiently, without incorporating real video data or additional post-training stages.

papers.title: Mitigating exposure bias in large language model distillation: an imitation learning approach
papers.summary: Abstract Knowledge distillation is recognized as a valuable model compression strategy that alleviates the computational burden of large language models while preserving performance. This strategy involves training a smaller model utilizing both real data and predictions from a more cumbersome model. Traditional distillation methods, however, are often compromised by exposure bias, which results from reliance on next-step prediction training loss. This bias emerges when models are tested in free-running mode, differing from their training regime and leading to a progressive drift in input distributions between testing and training phases. An analogous issue, known as ‘distributional shift’, has been effectively addressed in imitation learning through various methodologies. Therefore, this paper specifically tailors an imitation learning-based solution to a traditional knowledge distillation framework which inherently considers both real data and the teacher’s predictions as dual sources of expert demonstrations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated over five different test datasets, where it outperforms traditional benchmarks across all evaluation metrics. Specifically, it achieves superior results in perplexity, multi-token generation, and G-Eval score, indicating improvements in both predictive accuracy and alignment with human judgment in text quality. These results underscore the potential of this approach to effectively address exposure bias in large language model distillation.

papers.title: Post-Training is About States, Not Tokens: A State Distribution View of SFT, RL, and On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: Large language model post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and distillation are often analyzed through their loss functions: maximum likelihood, policy gradients, forward KL, reverse KL, or related objective-level variants. We study a complementary factor: the state distribution on which supervision is applied. For an autoregressive policy, a state is a prompt plus generated prefix. SFT trains on fixed dataset states, while RL and on-policy distillation (OPD) train on states induced by the current learner. We formalize post-training as state-distribution shaping and run a controlled smallscale study using Qwen3-0.6B-Base on GSM8K, with TruthfulQA and MMLU as retention evaluations. Our results show three phenomena. First, a mild SFT run improves GSM8K with little forgetting, while a stress SFT run causes substantial retention loss. Second, OPD from a degraded SFT teacher surpasses that teacher on GSM8K, TruthfulQA, and MMLU, despite using the teacher as its only supervision source. Third, a lightweight on-policy RL run improves GSM8K while preserving retention. These results support a state-centric view of post-training: the source and locality of training states can be as important as the form of the supervision signal.

papers.title: Multi-Rollout On-Policy Distillation via Peer Successes and Failures
papers.summary: Large language models are often post-trained with sparse verifier rewards, which indicate whether a sampled trajectory succeeds but provide limited guidance about where reasoning succeeds or fails. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers denser token-level supervision by training on student-generated trajectories, yet existing methods typically distill each rollout independently and ignore the other attempts sampled for the same prompt. We introduce Multi-Rollout On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), a peer-conditioned distillation framework that uses the student's local rollout group to construct more informative teacher signals. MOPD conditions the teacher on both successful and failed peer rollouts: successes provide positive evidence for valid reasoning patterns, while failures provide structured negative evidence about plausible mistakes to avoid. We study two peer-context constructions: positive peer imitation and contrastive success-failure conditioning. Experiments on competitive programming, mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and tool-use benchmarks show that MOPD consistently improves over standard on-policy baselines. Further teacher-signal analysis shows that mixed success-failure contexts better align teacher scores with verifier rewards, indicating that the gains arise from more faithful, instance-adaptive supervision. These results indicate that effective on-policy distillation should exploit the student's multi-rollout trial-and-error behavior rather than treating rollouts as isolated samples.

papers.title: Are Full Rollouts Necessary for On-Policy Distillation?
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher feedback along student-generated rollouts rather than fixed teacher traces and has emerged as a promising post-training paradigm. However, standard OPD typically generates full rollouts during training, which is computationally expensive and may expose the student to unreliable teacher feedback at late rollout positions, especially during early training. We identify the rollout horizon as a key bottleneck in OPD that substantially impacts training efficiency. Unlike Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), OPD does not require a final answer reward to provide learning signals. Therefore, full rollouts may not always be necessary for OPD. Motivated by this insight, we propose two simple horizon-control strategies: Progressive OPD (POPD), which gradually expands the rollout horizon during training, and Truncated OPD (TOPD), which permanently performs distillation on reliable truncated rollouts. Experiments on mathematical reasoning show that POPD improves the training efficiency of OPD by up to 3$\times$, while TOPD matches OPD performance using only 10\% of the rollout horizon, leading to substantial wall-clock and memory reductions. These results demonstrate that controlling the rollout horizon offers a simple and practical path to more efficient OPD.

papers.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.

papers.title: ErrOPD: When Does On-Policy Distillation Transfer Teacher Errors?
papers.summary: A distilled student can copy its teacher's mistakes along with its skills. On-policy distillation (OPD), used in recent post-training recipes, has the teacher grade every token of the student's own outputs. Which teacher errors does it pass on? We build ErrOPD, a testbed whose teachers are fine-tuned to close a JSON list one item early, an error their students almost never make. The answer depends on the KL direction: across four model families, forward-KL OPD transmits the error within the training budget (+13-23 points), while reverse-KL OPD at our reference learning rate adds under 0.05 points. A duplicated ID and, where the decision arises, two SQL errors show the same split. The reverse-KL update scales with the student's own probability of a token, and an intervention tests this: giving reverse KL forward KL's gradient magnitude at the error decision alone makes it transmit on two model pairs. Reverse-KL OPD can delay such errors rather than block them: some runs adopt the error with longer training, and Qwen3 students that already make it, even rarely, adopt it within the budget. Because greedy evaluation on Qwen3 misses the inherited error, distilled students should also be audited on sampled outputs.

ideas.title: Per-sample validity-gated data-source curriculum: on-policy only for rollouts that pass validity
ideas.description: Instead of a global switch, make the curriculum per sample. At each step the student generates rollouts for a fraction lambda of the batch. Rollouts the validity checker accepts are kept as on-policy prefixes with teacher token-level feedback. Invalid rollouts are either replaced by the off-policy (teacher or fixed) sequence for that input, or truncated at the first invalid position and continued with the teacher prefix. The effective on-policy fraction therefore rises automatically as the student improves, with no threshold to tune. The mechanism transfers instance-level curriculum ideas, which order examples by difficulty, to the choice of which policy generates each example's prefix. The variant is compared against the global adaptive switch, a constant lambda, and an inverted control that keeps only invalid rollouts. The inverted control tests whether on-policy value comes from correcting near-valid errors or from exposure to garbage.
ideas.gap: Gap 6: data-source curricula rather than instance-ordering curricula. It also addresses Gap 3, invalid rate as the primary metric.

hypothesis.claim: The useful on-policy signal for structural validity comes from student states that are near the valid manifold. Gating per sample on validity delivers that signal from the first steps, while filtering the unhelpful garbage states that hurt small students. It should beat constant mixing, and beat a global switch whose timing is coarse.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: The validity-gated arm with lambda=0.5 reaches val_invalid_rate at least 0.5 points below constant lambda=0.5 and below the 8.8 baseline. The keep-invalid-only control is worse than pure off-policy, and the realized on-policy fraction rises monotonically over training.

papers.title: Exploring and enhancing the transfer of distribution in knowledge distillation for autoregressive language models
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a technique that compresses large teacher models by training smaller student models to mimic them. The success of KD in auto-regressive language models mainly relies on Reverse KL for mode-seeking and student-generated output (SGO) to combat exposure bias. Our theoretical analyses and experimental validation reveal that while Reverse KL effectively mimics certain features of the teacher distribution, it fails to capture most of its behaviors. Conversely, SGO incurs higher computational costs and presents challenges in optimization, particularly when the student model is significantly smaller than the teacher model. These constraints are primarily due to the immutable distribution of the teacher model, which fails to adjust adaptively to models of varying sizes. We introduce Online Knowledge Distillation (OKD), where the teacher network integrates small online modules to concurrently train with the student model. This strategy abolishes the necessity for on-policy sampling and merely requires minimal updates to the parameters of the teacher's online module during training, thereby allowing dynamic adaptation to the student's distribution to make distillation better. Extensive results across multiple generation datasets show that OKD achieves or exceeds the performance of leading methods in various model architectures and sizes, reducing training time by up to fourfold.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Improving Autoregressive Training with Dynamic Oracles
papers.summary: Many tasks within NLP can be framed as sequential decision problems, ranging from sequence tagging to text generation. However, for many tasks, the standard training methods, including maximum likelihood (teacher forcing) and scheduled sampling, suffer from exposure bias and a mismatch between metrics employed during training and inference. DAgger provides a solution to mitigate these problems, yet it requires a metric-specific dynamic oracle algorithm, which does not exist for many common metrics like span-based F1, ROUGE, and BLEU. In this paper, we develop these novel dynamic oracles and show they maintain DAgger's no-regret guarantee for decomposable metrics like span-based F1. We evaluate the algorithm's performance on named entity recognition (NER), text summarization, and machine translation (MT). While DAgger with dynamic oracle yields less favorable results in our MT experiments, it outperforms the baseline techniques in NER and text summarization.

papers.title: Calibrated Progressive Distillation: Co-Designing Curriculum and Target Mixing for Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a key technique for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet it faces challenges stemming from the teacher-student capacity gap.While existing KD methods address these challenges either by mixing teacher and student distributions in the distillation target or by using curriculum learning to sequence training from easy to hard examples, they typically design these two strategies independently, missing the opportunity for synergistic co-design.To bridge this gap, we propose Calibrated Progressive Distillation (CPD), a white-box KD framework that co-designs curriculum scheduling and target mixing through a unified difficulty-aware principle.CPD uses a difficulty profile to select epoch-specific subsets that ensure a uniform increase in average difficulty, adapting to the dataset's intrinsic hardness structure.Simultaneously, the mixing coefficient in the distillation target and the distillation temperature are synchronized with this progression, gradually shifting supervision from teacher-dominated to student-informed signals as training advances.Theoretically, CPD ensures bounded gradients and induces an implicit attention shift from easy to hard samples.Empirically, CPD consistently outperforms advanced KD methods across diverse tasks, while reducing training runtime by over 10%.Our work demonstrates that aligning data scheduling with distillation signal design is crucial for effective and efficient LLM distillation.

We introduce Multi-Rollout On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), a peer-conditioned distillation framework that uses the student's local rollout group to construct more informative teacher signals. MOPD conditions the teacher on both successful and failed peer rollouts: successes provide positive evidence for valid reasoning patterns, while failures provide structured negative evidence about plausible mistakes to avoid. We study two peer-context constructions: positive peer imitation and contrastive success-failure conditioning. Experiments on competitive programming, mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and tool-use benchmarks show that MOPD consistently improves over standard on-policy baselines. Further teacher-signal analysis shows that mixed success-failure contexts better align teacher scores with verifier rewards, indicating that the gains arise from more faithful, instance-adaptive supervision. These results indicate that effective on-policy distillation should exploit the student's multi-rollout trial-and-error behavior rather than treating rollouts as isolated samples.

papers.title: Not Every Rollout Needs Distillation: Correctness-Filtered On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supervises student-generated trajectories with a reference-conditioned version of the same base model. We ask whether every trajectory supplies distinct supervision that warrants its distillation cost. Gradient measurements on Qwen3-1.7B at initialization reveal that correct and incorrect responses have similar individual gradient magnitudes, but incorrect responses have approximately three times the coherent gradient share. Their estimated population-mean directions also largely overlap. A signal--noise model fitted at a small group size tracks alignment at larger group sizes without refitting. Motivated by these measurements, we introduce correctness-filtered OPSD (C-OPSD), which generates one response per problem and distills only a subset of incorrect responses. Removing unselected rows before both distillation forwards avoids their teacher/student forward and student backward work. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD achieves on-par performance with full OPSD. In a measured micro-batch-size-four implementation, executed rows decrease by approximately 68%, and with retained rows packed into full micro-batches, training takes about 40% less time while rollout generation remains unchanged. Together, the measurements and training results connect outcome-conditioned supervision redundancy to more compute-efficient distillation.

papers.title: Teacher-student curriculum learning for reinforcement learning
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (rl) is a popular paradigm for sequential decision making problems. The past decade's advances in rl have led to breakthroughs in many challenging domains such as video games, board games, robotics, and chip design. The sample inefficiency of deep reinforcement learning methods is a significant obstacle when applying rl to real-world problems. Transfer learning has been applied to reinforcement learning such that the knowledge gained in one task can be applied when training in a new task. Curriculum learning is concerned with sequencing tasks or data samples such that knowledge can be transferred between those tasks to learn a target task that would otherwise be too difficult to solve. Designing a curriculum that improves sample efficiency is a complex problem. In this thesis, we propose a teacher-student curriculum learning setting where we simultaneously train a teacher that selects tasks for the student while the student learns how to solve the selected task. Our method is independent of human domain knowledge and manual curriculum design. We evaluated our methods on two reinforcement learning benchmarks: grid world and the challenging Google Football environment. With our method, we can improve the sample efficiency and generality of the student compared to tabula-rasa reinforcement learning.

papers.title: A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models
papers.summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) trains large language models with teacher guidance on student-generated trajectories, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the histories encountered during deployment. As its use expands across language model training, different formulations of supervision and optimization make it difficult to compare methods and understand when they are effective. This survey develops a unified view of OPD through the interplay between student-generated states, teacher information, and policy updates. This framework connects the foundations of distillation with self-distillation, multi-teacher integration, reinforcement learning, and interactive agents. We examine how these settings change the supervision available to the student and relate the resulting design choices to capability transfer, training efficiency, and deployment. Our synthesis centers on the conditions under which guidance remains reliable and learnable as the student evolves, considering both immediate performance and the capacity for subsequent learning. We conclude by discussing open challenges in adapting supervision and allocating computation to support effective learning.

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation with Curriculum Turn-level Guidance for Multi-turn Agents
papers.summary: Multi-turn agents that plan, invoke tools, and interact with environments offer a promising paradigm for solving complex tasks, yet their capabilities typically rely on very large models whose inference cost is prohibitive in practice.On-Policy Distillation (OPD) is a natural recipe for transferring such capabilities to smaller students, but we find that it suffers a characteristic failure mode in this setting: small student errors compound across turns and push the trajectory out of the teacher's familiar state distribution, so the teacher's supervision becomes least reliable precisely where the student needs it most.We propose Guided On-Policy Distillation (Guided-OPD), a simple yet effective algorithm that mixes teacher-and studentgenerated turns within each rollout and schedules the teacher's intervention probability along a curriculum that decays to zero.Strong guidance keeps early trajectories close to the teacher distribution and is then gradually withdrawn to recover the purely on-policy regime used at inference.On ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, distilling Qwen3 students from a Qwen3-30B-A3B teacher, Guided-OPD yields average relative gains of 21.1% in Score and 25.5% in Success Rate over vanilla OPD, with larger gains on smaller students.

handoff.topic: Invalid-rate-triggered off-to-on switch, with yoked-step and corrupted-prefix controls
handoff.guidance: Test this idea: A switch triggered by the student's own invalid rate achieves lower val_invalid_rate than pure off-policy, pure on-policy, and fixed-step switches. The benefit requires student-generated prefixes: corrupted-ground-truth prefixes at matched error rate should not reproduce it. (expected: Adaptive switch (best tau) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1.0 point below the better pure regime, averaged over 5 seeds, and below the 8.8 baseline. (B) on_policy_frac=1.0 throughout. (C) GKD-style static on_policy_frac=0.5. (D) fixed-step switches at 750, 1500 and 2250. Chosen idea: Invalid-rate-triggered off-to-on switch, with yoked-step and corrupted-prefix controls. Train the student off-policy at first (on_policy_frac=0, teacher or ground-truth prefixes). Then raise on_policy_frac to a target value (0.5 or 1.0) once the student's running free-run invalid rate, measured on a small held-out training probe batch every 100 steps, drops below a threshold tau. papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Mask Forcing: Improving Autoregressive Video Diffusion Distillation via Dual-Noise Masking Rollout
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have shown great potential in real-time video generation. Recent methods distill pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into causal AR students through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), but the generated videos often suffer from over-saturation and over-smoothing issues, resulting in limited visual quality and realism. The key contributing factor is the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL objective in DMD, which can cause the student distribution to collapse onto only a few modes of the teacher distribution. To address this, we propose Mask Forcing, a Dual-Noise Masking Rollout strategy that perturbs the AR student self-rollout to mitigate mode collapse induced by reverse-KL mode seeking. The core idea is to inject cleaner signals into noisy rollout inputs via random masks along spatial and temporal axes during the self-rollout process of AR diffusion distillation. Such perturbations encourage the student rollouts to explore more regions of the teacher distribution, allowing DMD to provide learning signals beyond the modes already covered by the student. Moreover, the cleaner tokens act as denoising guidance for other noisier tokens, improving the intermediate rollout predictions and reducing error accumulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method improves multiple AR video diffusion distillation methods with higher visual quality efficiently, without incorporating real video data or additional post-training stages.

papers.title: Mitigating exposure bias in large language model distillation: an imitation learning approach
papers.summary: Abstract Knowledge distillation is recognized as a valuable model compression strategy that alleviates the computational burden of large language models while preserving performance. This strategy involves training a smaller model utilizing both real data and predictions from a more cumbersome model. Traditional distillation methods, however, are often compromised by exposure bias, which results from reliance on next-step prediction training loss. This bias emerges when models are tested in free-running mode, differing from their training regime and leading to a progressive drift in input distributions between testing and training phases. An analogous issue, known as ‘distributional shift’, has been effectively addressed in imitation learning through various methodologies. Therefore, this paper specifically tailors an imitation learning-based solution to a traditional knowledge distillation framework which inherently considers both real data and the teacher’s predictions as dual sources of expert demonstrations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated over five different test datasets, where it outperforms traditional benchmarks across all evaluation metrics. Specifically, it achieves superior results in perplexity, multi-token generation, and G-Eval score, indicating improvements in both predictive accuracy and alignment with human judgment in text quality. These results underscore the potential of this approach to effectively address exposure bias in large language model distillation.

papers.title: DASH-OPD: Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: While on-policy distillation (OPD) reduces exposure bias by training student language models on their own rollouts, early student errors in long-horizon agentic scenarios can lead to contexts unfamiliar to the teacher. To improve trajectory quality, recent work on agentic OPD introduces teacher intervention into training rollouts by switching the executor between the student and the teacher. However, existing methods determine how much teacher intervention is needed---but not when. To address this limitation, we propose DASH-OPD (Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for OPD), the first agentic OPD method to perform adaptive, bidirectional executor switching. At each turn, DASH-OPD measures teacher--student discrepancy using a mean log-likelihood ratio over action tokens. High student-to-teacher ratios on student turns serve as drift signals, while low teacher-to-student ratios on teacher turns serve as recovery signals. These signals are accumulated over multiple turns to form drift and recovery evidence, respectively. DASH-OPD switches executors when either type of evidence exceeds its corresponding switching threshold, introducing hysteresis that prevents rapid switching triggered by transient discrepancy fluctuations. Across three benchmarks and two student model scales, DASH-OPD outperforms five baselines in all 14 task-performance comparisons, while requiring the fewest interaction turns in nine of ten efficiency comparisons. Code, trained models, and training logs are available at https://github.com/Lucian1115/DASH-OPD

papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.

direction.thesis: A schedule that starts off-policy, while the student's rollouts are mostly garbage, and switches to on-policy once rollouts are near-valid should beat both pure regimes. The best switch point should be tied to the student's own invalid rate rather than to a fixed step.
direction.steer_link: This turns the researcher's 'when does each work better' into a within-run question. Each regime may be best at a different training phase, so the answer could be 'both, in sequence'.
direction.gap: Gap 6: DAgger mixing and GKD's λ are static or simply annealed. Curricula order instances, never the policy that generates the training prefixes.
direction.open_question: Is there an optimal switch point? Does an adaptive trigger, such as switching when the student's batch invalid rate falls below a threshold, beat a fixed step?
direction.first_experiment: Edit the schedule so that on_policy_frac is 0 until step S and then 1. Sweep S over {0, 750, 1500, 2250, 3000} at the default size with 2 seeds, and compare val_invalid_rate against the two pure endpoints.
direction.risk: The curve over S is monotone, with one pure regime best throughout. This reduces to the plain comparison and yields only a minor tuning trick.

meta_review.text: Do not make an adaptive or state-triggered teacher/student switch the main contribution. DTDD, DASH-OPD and CPD already cover that ground. Build the idea around a control that isolates mechanism and would change how the field explains on-policy gains. Examples: a matched-error corrupted-prefix arm (the student's own errors versus generic noise), or a length-matched random-truncation arm (validity versus prefix length).

When proposing an adaptive trigger, include a yoked or replay arm that reruns each seed's adaptive switch step as a fixed schedule. Without it, a trigger 'win' cannot be told apart from simply landing on a good switch step.

Do not filter on-policy data in a way that discards the error-bearing states the method is supposed to correct, such as keeping only valid rollouts. Keep supervision at and before the first error, and check that the gate cannot collapse into pure off-policy for a weak student.

Stay inside existing edit scopes (the schedule knob, a cheap probe) where possible, and include a minimal low-run first test. If the idea needs new infrastructure, such as an incremental validity checker or teacher continuations from arbitrary prefixes, state its cost and give a fallback that does not weaken the test.

Size the claimed effect against seed noise. Small margins (0.3–0.5 points) on 3 seeds are judged unresolvable, so use 5 or more seeds or target larger effects. Also state novelty as provisional (abstract-level only) and list the full-text checks still needed, for example arXiv:2009.07253 and the learning-to-search roll-in/roll-out work.

idea.title: Invalid-rate-triggered off-to-on switch, with yoked-step and corrupted-prefix controls
idea.description: Train the student off-policy at first (on_policy_frac=0, teacher or ground-truth prefixes). Then raise on_policy_frac to a target value (0.5 or 1.0) once the student's running free-run invalid rate, measured on a small held-out training probe batch every 100 steps, drops below a threshold tau. Two controls test why the trigger works. The first is a yoked fixed-step control: for each seed, a separate run switches at the exact step where the adaptive run fired. If the yoked run matches the adaptive run, the trigger's only value is locating a good step offline. If the adaptive run is better, the online response to the student's own state matters. The second is a discriminating negative control aimed at the exposure-bias explanation. After the same trigger, the run replaces student rollouts with ground-truth prefixes that are randomly token-corrupted, at a rate matched to the student's current per-token error rate. If this matches true on-policy, the late-phase gain comes from generic prefix noise (a robustness effect) rather than from teacher correction of the student's own errors.
idea.gap: Gap 6 (schedules from off- to on-policy and when to switch), with secondary relevance to gap 3 (invalid rate as the primary metric).

hypothesis.claim: A switch triggered by the student's own invalid rate achieves lower val_invalid_rate than pure off-policy, pure on-policy, and fixed-step switches. The benefit requires student-generated prefixes: corrupted-ground-truth prefixes at matched error rate should not reproduce it.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Adaptive switch (best tau) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1.0 point below the better pure regime, averaged over 5 seeds, and below the 8.8 baseline. The yoked fixed-step run is within noise of or worse than adaptive. The corrupted-prefix control recovers less than half of the adaptive gain over pure off-policy.

idea.experiment_plan: Use default d_model=32, n_layers=2, steps=3000, lr=0.003, temperature=1.0, and 5 seeds per arm on multimodal-transduction-L6-A8. Arms: (A) on_policy_frac=0 throughout. (B) on_policy_frac=1.0 throughout. (C) GKD-style static on_policy_frac=0.5. (D) fixed-step switches at 750, 1500 and 2250. (E) adaptive trigger with tau in {40%, 25%, 15%} on a 256-example probe batch, switching to frac in {0.5, 1.0}; set a 1500-step cap and force the switch if the trigger has not fired. (F) yoked fixed-step switch at E's firing step, with a different seed. (G) the same trigger as E, but post-switch prefixes are ground truth with random token substitution at a rate matched to the student's measured per-token error. The loss stays the default divergence across all arms, so the sampling distribution is the only factor varied. Implement this as a schedule edit plus a data-source edit for G. Report the final val_invalid_rate, the invalid-rate trajectory and the trigger step. Count total forward passes so compute can be compared across arms.
idea.novelty_rationale: In the reviewed works, mixing between fixed and student data is static (GKD λ) or follows a simple anneal (DAgger-style). Curriculum work orders instances rather than the data-generating policy. None of these papers conditions the switch on the student's own validity, separates trigger responsiveness from step location with a yoked control, or tests corrupted prefixes against student prefixes at matched error rate. Mask Forcing perturbs rollouts in video only. This is based on the reviewed set, not an exhaustive search.

design.mechanism: Early student rollouts are mostly invalid, so on-policy supervision then lands on states that are irrelevant once training converges, and gives noisy gradients. Once rollouts are near-valid, the student-visited states overlap the states it will reach at test time. Teacher correction on those states then reduces compounding structural errors.
design.intervention: A schedule edit raises on_policy_frac from 0 to a target value when the probe-batch invalid rate falls below tau. A data-source edit for control G substitutes corrupted ground-truth prefixes.
assumptions: The train script exposes a teacher that can score student-sampled prefixes when on_policy_frac>0.
Probe-batch invalid rate is cheap enough to compute every 100 steps and tracks val_invalid_rate.
Five seeds give seed variance small enough to resolve a gap of about 1 point.
design.minimal_test: Run 3 seeds each of: pure off-policy, pure on-policy, fixed switch at 1500, and adaptive with tau=25% and frac=1.0, plus one yoked and one corrupted-prefix run per seed. That is 18 short runs.
design.kill_criterion: Abandon the idea if adaptive is not better than the best of the pure and fixed-step arms by more than one seed-standard-deviation, or if the yoked control matches adaptive and the corrupted-prefix control matches on-policy. In that case, report that timing and generic noise explain the effect.
confound_controls: Yoked fixed-step switch at the adaptive firing step separates online responsiveness from step location.
Corrupted ground-truth prefixes at matched error rate separate student-specific error correction from generic prefix noise.
Divergence, temperature, lr and steps are held fixed across arms, so the sampling distribution is not confounded with the loss.
Total forward passes, including rollout cost, are reported for compute-matched comparison.
design.resource_risk: The model is tiny, so even with 5 seeds the roughly 40 runs are cheap. The main risk is the trigger never firing within 1500 steps at low tau, which the forced-switch cap handles.

novelty_review.summary: Two retrieved papers not cited in the candidate's sources, DASH-OPD (arXiv:2607.29078) and DTDD (arXiv:2610.19302), already use adaptive triggers based on the student's state to decide when the teacher intervenes in on-policy distillation. However, those triggers act within rollouts: per-turn executor switching or segment-level teacher takeover. They use teacher-student discrepancy signals, not a training-schedule-level switch of on_policy_frac driven by a free-run invalid rate. Their abstracts also do not describe a yoked fixed-step control or a matched-error corrupted-prefix control. GKD, the imitation-learning KD papers and Mask Forcing share the exposure-bias motivation, or the idea of perturbing rollouts, but not the adaptive global switch. The instance-level curriculum paper is only lexically related. On abstract evidence alone, the specific combination looks provisionally distinct, but the adaptive-trigger idea itself has close prior art.

papers.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to reduce its inference cost and memory footprint, by training a smaller student model. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models suffer from distribution mismatch between output sequences seen during training and those generated by the student during inference. To address this issue, we introduce Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Instead of solely relying on a fixed set of output sequences, GKD trains the student on its self-generated output sequences by leveraging feedback from the teacher on such sequences. Unlike supervised KD approaches, GKD also offers the flexibility to employ alternative loss functions between the student and teacher, which can be useful when the student lacks the expressivity to mimic the teacher's distribution. Furthermore, GKD facilitates the seamless integration of distillation with RL fine-tuning (RLHF). We demonstrate the efficacy of GKD for distilling auto-regressive language models on summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning tasks, and task-agnostic distillation for instruction-tuning.

papers.title: Autoregressive Knowledge Distillation through Imitation Learning
papers.summary: The performance of autoregressive models on natural language generation tasks has dramatically improved due to the adoption of deep, self-attentive architectures.However, these gains have come at the cost of hindering inference speed, making state-of-the-art models cumbersome to deploy in real-world, timesensitive settings.We develop a compression technique for autoregressive models that is driven by an imitation learning perspective on knowledge distillation.The algorithm is designed to address the exposure bias problem.On prototypical language generation tasks such as translation and summarization, our method consistently outperforms other distillation algorithms, such as sequence-level knowledge distillation.Student models trained with our method attain 1.4 to 4.8 BLEU/ROUGE points higher than those trained from scratch, while increasing inference speed by up to 14 times in comparison to the teacher model. 1

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. Instead, we argue that the compact student network should be guided gradually using samples ordered in a meaningful sequence. Thus, it can bridge the gap of feature representation between the teacher and student network step by step. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.title: Mask Forcing: Improving Autoregressive Video Diffusion Distillation via Dual-Noise Masking Rollout
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have shown great potential in real-time video generation. Recent methods distill pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into causal AR students through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), but the generated videos often suffer from over-saturation and over-smoothing issues, resulting in limited visual quality and realism. The key contributing factor is the mode-seeking behavior of the reverse KL objective in DMD, which can cause the student distribution to collapse onto only a few modes of the teacher distribution. To address this, we propose Mask Forcing, a Dual-Noise Masking Rollout strategy that perturbs the AR student self-rollout to mitigate mode collapse induced by reverse-KL mode seeking. The core idea is to inject cleaner signals into noisy rollout inputs via random masks along spatial and temporal axes during the self-rollout process of AR diffusion distillation. Such perturbations encourage the student rollouts to explore more regions of the teacher distribution, allowing DMD to provide learning signals beyond the modes already covered by the student. Moreover, the cleaner tokens act as denoising guidance for other noisier tokens, improving the intermediate rollout predictions and reducing error accumulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method improves multiple AR video diffusion distillation methods with higher visual quality efficiently, without incorporating real video data or additional post-training stages.

papers.title: Mitigating exposure bias in large language model distillation: an imitation learning approach
papers.summary: Abstract Knowledge distillation is recognized as a valuable model compression strategy that alleviates the computational burden of large language models while preserving performance. This strategy involves training a smaller model utilizing both real data and predictions from a more cumbersome model. Traditional distillation methods, however, are often compromised by exposure bias, which results from reliance on next-step prediction training loss. This bias emerges when models are tested in free-running mode, differing from their training regime and leading to a progressive drift in input distributions between testing and training phases. An analogous issue, known as ‘distributional shift’, has been effectively addressed in imitation learning through various methodologies. Therefore, this paper specifically tailors an imitation learning-based solution to a traditional knowledge distillation framework which inherently considers both real data and the teacher’s predictions as dual sources of expert demonstrations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated over five different test datasets, where it outperforms traditional benchmarks across all evaluation metrics. Specifically, it achieves superior results in perplexity, multi-token generation, and G-Eval score, indicating improvements in both predictive accuracy and alignment with human judgment in text quality. These results underscore the potential of this approach to effectively address exposure bias in large language model distillation.

papers.title: DASH-OPD: Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: While on-policy distillation (OPD) reduces exposure bias by training student language models on their own rollouts, early student errors in long-horizon agentic scenarios can lead to contexts unfamiliar to the teacher. To improve trajectory quality, recent work on agentic OPD introduces teacher intervention into training rollouts by switching the executor between the student and the teacher. However, existing methods determine how much teacher intervention is needed---but not when. To address this limitation, we propose DASH-OPD (Discrepancy-Aware Switching with Hysteresis for OPD), the first agentic OPD method to perform adaptive, bidirectional executor switching. At each turn, DASH-OPD measures teacher--student discrepancy using a mean log-likelihood ratio over action tokens. High student-to-teacher ratios on student turns serve as drift signals, while low teacher-to-student ratios on teacher turns serve as recovery signals. These signals are accumulated over multiple turns to form drift and recovery evidence, respectively. DASH-OPD switches executors when either type of evidence exceeds its corresponding switching threshold, introducing hysteresis that prevents rapid switching triggered by transient discrepancy fluctuations. Across three benchmarks and two student model scales, DASH-OPD outperforms five baselines in all 14 task-performance comparisons, while requiring the fewest interaction turns in nine of ten efficiency comparisons. Code, trained models, and training logs are available at https://github.com/Lucian1115/DASH-OPD

papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.

idea.title: Invalid-rate-triggered switch from off-policy to on-policy distillation versus fixed-step switches
idea.description: Turn GKD's static student-data fraction into a feedback-controlled schedule. Training starts fully off-policy (on_policy_frac=0, word-level KD on fixed or teacher prefixes). Every 50 steps the script measures the invalid rate of a small batch of student rollouts generated at the training temperature. When that rollout invalid rate stays below a threshold tau for two consecutive checks, on_policy_frac ramps over 200 steps to a target lambda_on. The mechanism comes from DAgger's mixing coefficient beta in imitation-learning KD, which decides when the learner's own states are good enough to supervise. Here beta is driven by a measured competence signal rather than decayed by step count. The comparison set has three groups: (a) pure off-policy, (b) pure on-policy at several fractions, and (c) fixed-step switches at 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000 steps. This tests whether the switch time matters, and whether tying it to the student's own invalid rate beats a well-chosen fixed step.
idea.gap: Gap 6: schedules from off- to on-policy, including when to switch. It also touches Gap 3, invalid rate as the primary metric.

hypothesis.claim: On-policy supervision helps only once student rollouts are near-valid. Earlier, garbage prefixes waste teacher signal, as the capacity-gap difficulty reported in arXiv:2409.12512 suggests. A switch triggered by rollout invalid rate should therefore beat both pure regimes and match or beat the best fixed-step switch without per-task tuning.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Adaptive switch (tau of about 0.3, lambda_on of 0.5) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1 point below the better pure regime and below the 8.8 baseline. Across 3 seeds it is within 0.3 of, or better than, the best fixed switch step, while the worst fixed step is at least 1 point worse.

idea.experiment_plan: Edit the schedule in the train script: add an every-50-step rollout validity probe of 64 samples and a ramp of on_policy_frac. Keep the loss fixed (the default divergence) and temperature at 1.0, and use defaults lr=0.003, d_model=32, n_layers=2, steps=3000. Arms: on_policy_frac constant at 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0; fixed switch to 0.5 at steps 500, 1000, 1500 and 2000; adaptive tau in {0.2, 0.4, 0.6}. Run 3 seeds each, 33 runs in total. Report final val_invalid_rate, the step at which the adaptive trigger fired, and the student rollout invalid rate curve. Count probe rollouts toward the compute budget.
idea.novelty_rationale: GKD uses a fixed or simply annealed lambda, and the imitation-learning KD papers decay mixing by schedule. None of the reviewed papers conditions the data-source switch on a measured student validity signal or compares it against a sweep of fixed switch points. Whether such a trigger already exists elsewhere is unverified; see the novelty queries.

idea.title: Invalid-rate-triggered switch from SeqKD to on-policy distillation versus fixed-step switches
idea.description: Training starts fully off-policy (on_policy_frac=0, teacher-generated or ground-truth prefixes). A running estimate of the student's batch invalid rate on its own greedy rollouts is tracked every 50 steps. When it falls below a threshold tau, on_policy_frac is ramped to a target value lambda_on over a short window. This adaptive trigger is compared against a grid of fixed-step switches and against both pure regimes. The proposed mechanism is that early on-policy rollouts are mostly malformed, so teacher feedback on them is spent on states the converged student never visits; that gradient is off-target and noisy. Once rollouts are near-valid, the states the student visits overlap with its eventual test-time states, and only then does exposure-bias correction pay off. If this is right, the best switch point should line up with a student invalid-rate level, not with a step count.
idea.gap: Gap 6 (off-to-on data-source schedules and when to switch), and as a side effect gap 3 (invalid rate as the primary metric).

hypothesis.claim: A schedule that switches from off- to on-policy when the student's own rollout invalid rate drops below a threshold gives lower val_invalid_rate than pure off-policy, pure on-policy, and the best fixed-step switch. The optimal fixed switch step should move with student capacity in a way that the invalid-rate trigger tracks automatically.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Adaptive trigger (tau around 30%) reaches val_invalid_rate at least 1.0 point below the best of {pure off, pure on, best fixed switch}, averaged over 5 seeds, and beats the 8.8 baseline. Across d_model in {16,32,64}, the best fixed switch step varies by more than 2x, while the best tau varies by at most one grid level.

idea.experiment_plan: Edit the schedule so that on_policy_frac(t) is a function of the monitored invalid rate. Every 50 steps, greedy-decode 64 training inputs with the student and score them with the task validity checker. Arms, with 5 seeds each, steps=3000, and lr/temperature at defaults unless stated: (a) on_policy_frac=0; (b) on_policy_frac=1 from step 0; (c) constant on_policy_frac=0.5; (d) fixed switch at steps {300,750,1500,2250}, ramping 0 to 1 over 100 steps; (e) adaptive trigger with tau in {60,30,15}% and the same ramp; (f) a matched control that replays the switch step each seed of arm (e) actually used, but as a fixed step. Arm (f) separates the benefit of the trigger's timing from its per-seed adaptivity. Repeat (a), (b), (d-best) and (e-best) at d_model {16,64} to test whether the optimum moves with capacity. Use the same loss in every arm (token-level FKL on teacher logits at temperature 1) so the divergence is held fixed. Report val_invalid_rate, the switch step, and wall-clock.
idea.novelty_rationale: GKD uses a fixed lambda, and the DAgger-style KD in [arXiv:2009.07253] uses a fixed or annealed mixing. Neither conditions the data source on the student's measured rollout quality, nor reports how the switch point depends on capacity. Absence in this review does not prove it is untried elsewhere; the novelty queries below target that.

novelty_review.summary:
From the abstracts alone, no retrieved paper gates the off-to-on-policy data-source fraction on the student's measured rollout invalid rate, or tests whether the switch point tracks capacity. This is only a provisional difference, not verified novelty.

The closest overlap is DTDD. It shares the core mechanistic premise: on-policy supervision is unreliable when the student strays far from the teacher. It also uses an adaptive, student-state-based trigger. However, DTDD triggers teacher takeover inside rollouts based on divergence, rather than scheduling the data-source mix on validity.

Other overlaps are partial:
- GKD and the imitation-learning KD papers share the exposure-bias rationale for on-policy data.
- CPD and POCL share progressive teacher-to-student scheduling, but schedule on difficulty or fixed intervals.
- OKD supports the capacity-dependence assumption.

The abstracts do not reveal whether GKD's lambda or DAgger-style mixing is fixed, annealed or adaptive. The novelty rationale's claims about them need full-text checking.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation via Instance-level Sequence Learning
papers.summary: Recently, distillation approaches are suggested to extract general knowledge from a teacher network to guide a student network. Most of the existing methods transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student via feeding the sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the data. In this work, we provide a curriculum learning knowledge distillation framework via instance-level sequence learning. It employs the student network of the early epoch as a snapshot to create a curriculum for the student network's next training phase. We carry out extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and CINIC-10 datasets. Compared with several state-of-the-art methods, our framework achieves the best performance with fewer iterations.

papers.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a key technique for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet it faces challenges stemming from the teacher-student capacity gap.While existing KD methods address these challenges either by mixing teacher and student distributions in the distillation target or by using curriculum learning to sequence training from easy to hard examples, they typically design these two strategies independently, missing the opportunity for synergistic co-design.To bridge this gap, we propose Calibrated Progressive Distillation (CPD), a white-box KD framework that co-designs curriculum scheduling and target mixing through a unified difficulty-aware principle.CPD uses a difficulty profile to select epoch-specific subsets that ensure a uniform increase in average difficulty, adapting to the dataset's intrinsic hardness structure.Simultaneously, the mixing coefficient in the distillation target and the distillation temperature are synchronized with this progression, gradually shifting supervision from teacher-dominated to student-informed signals as training advances.Theoretically, CPD ensures bounded gradients and induces an implicit attention shift from easy to hard samples.Empirically, CPD consistently outperforms advanced KD methods across diverse tasks, while reducing training runtime by over 10%.Our work demonstrates that aligning data scheduling with distillation signal design is crucial for effective and efficient LLM distillation.

Finally, we show that SLaM comes with theoretical guarantees; along the way we give an algorithm improving the best-known sample complexity for learning halfspaces with margin under random classification noise, and provide the first convergence analysis for so-called ``forward loss-adjustment" methods.

papers.title: Being Strong Progressively! Enhancing Knowledge Distillation of Large Language Models through a Curriculum Learning Framework
papers.summary: Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses large language models (LLMs) by transferring the teacher model's capabilities to a smaller student model, reducing inference cost and memory usage while maintaining performance. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of sorted training samples in KD for LLMs. More generally, our work demonstrates how to structure training data within the KD process to enhance the stability and performance of distilled LLMs.

idea.title: Valid-prefix-truncated mixed rollouts: a token-level self-pacing off-to-on curriculum
idea.description: This replaces the global switch with a per-example curriculum. Each rollout is sampled from the student, but only up to its first position where the prefix becomes invalid; the checker is applied incrementally. From that position the teacher continues the sequence, and the student is trained with teacher-logit FKL on the whole spliced sequence. Early in training most of each sequence is teacher-generated, which is effectively off-policy. As the student improves, the student-generated fraction grows automatically, so the data source shifts from off- to on-policy at the granularity of each example. The mechanism under test is that garbage tails of student rollouts, not student prefixes in general, are what make early on-policy training harmful. A random-truncation control at matched student-prefix length distinguishes 'validity-aware truncation' from 'shorter student prefixes'.
idea.gap: Gap 6 (data-source curriculum, here per-token), and it also probes gap 7 (prefix perturbation or correction in discrete on-policy distillation).

hypothesis.claim: Truncating student rollouts at the first invalid prefix and splicing in teacher continuations lowers val_invalid_rate below both pure regimes and below a global invalid-rate-triggered switch. The benefit comes specifically from removing post-error states, not from shortening the student prefix.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Validity-truncated splicing beats pure off-policy by at least 1.5 points and pure on-policy by a wider margin. The random-truncation arm with matched student-prefix length recovers less than half of that gain. The student-prefix fraction rises monotonically during training without being scheduled.

idea.experiment_plan: Edit the augmentation/loss so that each training batch is built from student samples (temperature knob in {0.7,1.0}). Run the validity checker on prefixes and truncate at the first violation; if the task checker only scores full sequences, use the earliest position at which no valid completion exists under the task grammar. Then append a teacher greedy continuation and apply token-level FKL to teacher logits over all positions. Arms, 5 seeds each, d_model=32, steps=3000: (a) pure off (on_policy_frac=0); (b) pure on (on_policy_frac=1); (c) the best global switch from idea 1, or a fixed switch at 1500 if idea 1 is not yet run; (d) valid-prefix splicing; (e) random-truncation splicing, cutting each rollout at a position drawn from the per-step empirical distribution of arm (d)'s cut points; (f) splicing but with the loss masked to the student-prefix positions only, to test whether the teacher tail itself contributes. Log the student-prefix fraction over time and val_invalid_rate. Optionally repeat (a), (b), (d) and (e) at d_model=16, where the capacity gap is larger.
idea.novelty_rationale: DAgger-style KD and GKD use whole student rollouts or whole fixed sequences. Mask Forcing perturbs rollouts with noise in continuous video. None of the reviewed papers truncates discrete rollouts at a structural-validity boundary and hands control to the teacher, or controls with random truncation at matched length. Novelty is unverified beyond this review.
